title: Designed to Be Read
sub: Grades 5–8 · Art · Graphic design and type
objective: Students will look at the exhibition’s two posters, *The Writing Revolution* and *QWERTY’s Accidental Empire*, as graphic design. They will name the choices the posters share (bold color blocks, a thin white frame line that breaks off at a corner, tall condensed capitals, typewriter type and a black typewriter photograph), see how size, color and contrast lead the eye, compare kinds of type, and design a third poster for the series.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Everything you read was designed by someone. Seeing their choices helps you read more closely and make work of your own that people want to read.

items.text: describe the design choices in the exhibition’s posters: color blocks, frame, type and image
items.question: describe the color, frame, type and image choices in the posters?

items.text: explain how a designer uses size, color and contrast to lead the eye (visual hierarchy)
items.question: explain how size, color and contrast lead the eye?

items.text: compare serif, sans-serif and monospace type, and the mood each sets
items.question: tell serif, sans-serif and monospace type apart, and say what each feels like?

items.text: design a third poster in the same series, and explain each choice
items.question: design a poster that belongs to the series, and explain your choices?

materials: The two posters on page 3, projected or printed in color
The Typing Station on the exhibition website, to try the iMac’s fonts
Differentiated handouts, one per student; colored pencils or markers
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** look at both posters on screen, then open the Typing Station and set the line *The keyboard beneath your fingers holds a 150-year-old secret.* in each of the iMac’s fonts. Which font would you choose for a poster, and why?

steps.title: Where does your eye go?
script: Show *The Writing Revolution* poster and give students thirty seconds of silence. Ask: *“Where does your eye go first? Second? Third?”* Most will say the title, then the typewriter, then the text. Ask what made them look there: size, color, contrast. Name the idea: **visual hierarchy**.

screen.caption: The Writing Revolution, one of the exhibition’s two posters

steps.purpose: Look before naming anything: notice how the poster leads the eye.
students: Where does your eye go first? Second? Third?

steps.title: A pair
script: Show the two posters side by side. Ask: *“What do the two posters share? What makes them a pair?”* Build the list on page 3 together: two color blocks, a white frame line that breaks off at a corner, tall condensed capitals, typewriter text, the Urania typewriter. Name it: a **design system**, a set of rules that makes separate pieces look like a family.

Point out the differences: the colors change, and on *The Writing Revolution* the typewriter runs off the edge (a **bleed**) while on *QWERTY’s Accidental Empire* it sits whole on the cyan. Ask what each choice does.

steps.purpose: Find the rules both posters follow: a design system.
students: What do the two posters share? What makes them a pair?
What is different, and why might the designer have changed it?

steps.title: Anyone can design
script: Read: *“Desktop publishing software like PageMaker (1985) ended publishers' monopoly—suddenly, anyone could design newsletters, magazines, or books from their home.”* Open the iMac at the Typing Station and set the same line in its fonts: Times · Helvetica · Courier · Palatino · Antonio. Name the three kinds: **serif** (small strokes at the ends of letters), **sans-serif** (without them), **monospace** (every letter the same width, like a typewriter). Ask which font looks most like the posters’ titles.

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three end with a poster design for the series.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Number what they see first, second and third, match three kinds of type to their descriptions, and sketch a poster using a checklist of the series’ rules.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Compare the two posters in a table, explain the poster’s hierarchy, and plan a poster in three thumbnail sketches.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Write the rules of the design system, explain the bleed and the broken frame, and design a third poster with a designer’s note.

steps.purpose: Read the posters’ design, then design in the same system.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three end with a poster design of your own.

steps.title: Borrow a choice
script: Students hold up their designs. Ask: *“Which design choice from the posters would you borrow for your own work, and why?”* Ask a Red Level student to read their designer’s note.

screen.question: Which design choice from the posters would you borrow for your own work, and why?

steps.purpose: Have students name one design decision as a tool they now own.

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level reader.
